The retrieved evidence supports the Silurian as a period of major terrestrial plant innovation, with the first fungi and small vascular plants (such as Cooksonia) appearing on land during this era [d1][d2]. However, the earliest radiation of land plants (embryophytes) is traced to the Middle Ordovician to early Silurian transition (~470–430 Ma), suggesting that while the Silurian was a period of significant plant evolution, it may not have been the absolute birth moment of the first land plants [d3]. These conflicting timelines are further nuanced by the existence of complex plants like Baragwanathia with leaves and vascular tissue found in Silurian rocks, which challenges the widespread acceptance of Cooksonia as the sole first land plant [d2], and the broader context of Silurian representing a distinct but not uniquely defining phase in the transition to land [d4][d5].
[[END-OF-ANSWER]]
